content.intro: In this lesson, you will study primitive and reference variables in memory with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you choose types and variable scope deliberately instead of relying on guesses about values. In this lesson, focus on values versus references and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A reference identifies an object; assigning a reference copies the reference value, not the whole object. Two variables may therefore refer to the same mutable object. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect values versus references with assignment behavior before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Why Java is always pass-by-value
items.text: Java variables have declared or inferred static types and a defined scope. Local `var` infers a compile-time type from the initializer; it does not make the language dynamically typed. Apply that reasoning specifically to why java is always pass-by-value and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.
